questions.q: What does pg_hba.conf control, per this lesson?
options: Which clients are allowed to connect, from where, and using what authentication method
The amount of shared memory allocated to shared_buffers
Which tables are automatically vacuumed
The default tablespace for new databases
questions.explain: pg_hba.conf is PostgreSQL's host-based authentication file, controlling connection authorization and authentication method per rule.

questions.q: How does pg_hba.conf decide which rule applies to an incoming connection, per this lesson?
options: Rules are read top to bottom, and the first matching line wins
All matching rules are applied simultaneously and combined
Only the last line in the file is ever evaluated
Rules are selected at random for load balancing
questions.explain: pg_hba.conf rules are evaluated in order, top to bottom, and the first line that matches the connection attempt is the one that applies.

questions.q: Why might a default PostgreSQL install be unreachable from another machine even with the firewall open and pg_hba.conf correctly configured, per this lesson?
options: listen_addresses in postgresql.conf may default to localhost, so the postmaster isn't listening on external interfaces
PostgreSQL never accepts remote connections under any configuration
pg_hba.conf changes always require a full server restart to take effect
postgresql.conf and pg_hba.conf must always be identical files
questions.explain: listen_addresses controls which network interfaces the postmaster listens on; a localhost-only default blocks remote connections regardless of pg_hba.conf or firewall settings.

questions.q: What does the scram-sha-256 authentication method in pg_hba.conf represent, per this lesson?
options: The modern, stronger password-based authentication method, recommended over older md5
A method that trusts any connection with no password at all
A certificate-only authentication method with no password support
An authentication method exclusive to local Unix-domain socket connections
questions.explain: scram-sha-256 is described as the modern, stronger password-based authentication method, in contrast to the older md5 method and the unauthenticated trust method.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call pg_hba.conf's rule granularity genuinely distinctive compared to SQL Server or Oracle?
options: SQL Server uses a single server-wide authentication mode toggle, and Oracle lacks a comparable per-source-address rule file
SQL Server and Oracle both have an identical line-by-line authentication rule file
PostgreSQL is the only platform in the course that supports password authentication at all
SQL Server and Oracle do not support restricting connections by IP address under any mechanism
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts pg_hba.conf's per-database/user/address/method rules with SQL Server's single Windows/mixed authentication toggle and Oracle's listener/account-based approach.
